readerTitle: The rent is due even when nobody comes in
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점 원예 코너, 가구 공방) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 비용을 볼 때는 '얼마인가'보다 '이 결정을 하면 실제로 사라지는가'를 먼저 묻는다. 고정비와 변동비는 결정과 기간에 따라 나뉜다.
misconception: 보고서에서 적자인 부문을 닫거나 '원가'보다 싼 외주를 쓰면 그만큼 이익이 늘어난다.

sources.text: 관리회계의 표준 개념 (고정비·변동비 구분, 회피 가능 원가, 제조·구매 결정)

factChecks.note: 원예 코너 계산: 매출 $6,000 − 상품 $3,600 − 시간제 인력 $1,000 = $1,400. 배분된 임대료·매니저 급여 $2,200을 빼면 −$800(보고서상 적자). 코너를 닫아도 $2,200은 남으므로 매장 전체 이익은 $1,400 감소.
가구 공방 계산: 목재·부품 $40 + 시간제 조립 인건비 $25 = 회피 가능 원가 $65. 배분된 임대료·기계 $35를 더하면 보고서상 원가 $100. 외주가 $80 − $65 = 프레임당 $15 더 비쌈(임대료와 기계 비용이 그대로 남는다는 가정).
고정비·변동비 구분 예시(임대료, 보험, 급여제 매니저 = 고정 / 재고, 포장, 카드 수수료, 물량에 맞춘 시간제 인력 = 변동)는 일반적 분류이며, 계약 조건에 따라 달라질 수 있음을 카드에 밝혔습니다.

cards.title: The rent is due even when nobody comes in
body: Your hardware store's monthly report says the garden corner loses $800 a month.
Closing it looks like an easy way to earn $800 more. Before you do, follow where the money actually goes.

image.label: Zero sales today. Rent is still due.
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 철물점 안쪽의 원예 코너(화분, 흙 포대, 물뿌리개). 코너 위에 빨간 "−$800" 표지판. 매장 천장 위로 "Rent"라고 적힌 큰 지붕이 매장 전체를 덮고 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Close the garden corner?
body: The corner sells $6,000 a month. Plants and supplies cost $3,600. Part-time staff hours for it cost $1,000. The report also gives it $2,200 as its share of rent and the manager's salary. Result: −$800.
Your lease and manager stay either way. If you close the corner, what happens to the store's total profit?

options.feedback: That only works if the $2,200 of rent and salary disappears with the corner. It doesn't, so the other sections would have to carry it.
Right. The corner leaves $1,400 after its own costs, and that money was helping pay the rent. Close it and the $1,400 is gone, but the rent isn't.
Good instinct that the report's loss isn't real savings. But the corner was adding money, not breaking even, so closing it costs you.

cards.title: Split the costs that leave from the ones that stay.
body: The −$800 is real on paper. But **$2,200 of it stays** whether the corner exists or not. What closing actually removes is the $1,400 the corner brings in.

cards.title: Fixed vs variable costs
body: **Fixed costs** stay the same no matter how much you sell in a period: rent, insurance, a salaried manager, loan payments.
**Variable costs** rise and fall with each sale or each unit you make: stock, materials, packaging, card fees, hourly staff booked to match demand.
Reports often spread fixed costs across products to show a full "cost." That is useful for pricing, but it hides which costs a decision can actually change.
cards.softwareNote: Servers, payment fees and support per customer are mostly variable. Engineering salaries are mostly fixed. Cutting a little-used feature saves little unless the team shrinks or moves to other work.

cards.title: One question sorts most costs.
body: Ask: *If I sold nothing next month, would I still pay this?*
list: **Yes, in full:** fixed. Rent, insurance, software subscriptions, salaried staff.
**No:** variable. Stock, materials, shipping, sales commissions.
**Partly:** mixed. Electricity, a delivery van, staff with a minimum number of hours. Split these into the part that stays and the part that moves.
cards.callout: Mixed costs are common. Splitting them roughly is better than calling them all one thing.

cards.title: "Fixed" depends on the time window.
body: This month, your rent is fixed. When the lease is up for renewal, it becomes a choice. A smaller shop or a sublet could make it shrink.
The same goes for salaries, machines and contracts. Over a week, almost everything is fixed. Over five years, almost everything can change.
So the useful question is not "Is this cost fixed?" but **"Is it fixed for this decision, over this period?"**

image.label: Timeline where costs turn from locked to unlocked
image.brief: 가로 타임라인 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "This month"에는 "Rent", "Manager", "Machines" 아이콘에 자물쇠가 잠겨 있고, 오른쪽 "Lease renewal", "Next year"로 갈수록 자물쇠가 하나씩 열림. 깔끔한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Fixed costs still have to be paid.
body: Ignoring fixed costs for one decision doesn't make them free. Across the whole business, sales must cover them, or you lose money every month.
Space has value too. If a better product or a paying tenant could use the garden corner, its $1,400 must be compared with that option, not with zero.
And if closing the corner lets you move to a smaller store, part of the rent becomes a cost you can avoid.

cards.title: Now it's a furniture workshop.
body: Your report says each chair frame costs $100: wood and hardware $40, hourly assembly labor $25, and $35 as its share of the workshop lease and machines.
A supplier offers to make the frames for $80 each. Your lease and machines would stay. What do you do?

options.feedback: Only $65 per frame goes away when you stop making them. Paying $80 instead costs $15 more per frame, and the lease is still due.

options.text: Decline for now, unless the freed space and machines can earn money elsewhere
options.feedback: You keep the cheaper option today. If the space could take on more profitable work or the lease could shrink, the math changes and outsourcing may win.

options.text: Accept for half the frames to test the supplier
options.feedback: Testing a backup supplier has real value. But each outsourced frame still costs $15 more, so treat it as the price of the test.

cards.title: Before you cut, ask which costs actually go away.
body: A cost per unit mixes costs that leave with the decision and costs that stay. Only the ones that leave belong in the comparison.
**Try it today:** list your ten biggest monthly costs. Next to each, write F, V or M (mixed) using one question: would I still pay this if I sold nothing next month?
